english: By “heaps” there he means the hills, so that he can say: You do not know what existed before creation. Chapter 16, verses 18 and 19: “Earth, do not cover over the blood of my flesh, and let there be no place for my cry; and now behold, my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is in the highest.” Perplexed, he speaks to the earth, and calling on it for sympathy he says words that are also spoken as a prayer. He says: Do not be silent, earth, about what has happened to me, and do not hide the blood that is unjustly poured out from my flesh through its discharges. Do not let it stand in one place and be hidden, and do not let the things concerning my laments come to oblivion. “And let many,” he says, “be built up through my trials.” Or: Let the earth not hide my blood, but let it call on God for vengeance, since it holds the discharges of my body as witnesses. And let the air not hold back my cry, but let the force of my voice reach the heavens, so that God, standing as avenger of the evils that have happened and punishing those responsible, may in this way show to all the blamelessness of the life I have lived. And the words “Behold, my witness is in heaven” come from a most pure conscience. Chapter 19, verse 3: “Know only that the Lord has made me thus.” He brings them into fear, as if saying: Do not trample on me in my suffering in this way, and do not fall into the same things yourselves, since you share the same nature. Verses 4 and 5: “Yes indeed, in truth I have gone astray; error lodges with me, to speak words that should not be spoken, and my words wander and are not in season. But let it be that you magnify yourselves against me and leap upon me with reproach.” Let it be granted, he says, as a hypothesis, that I have gone astray. “Error lodges with me”—error is the devil. What harm, he says, comes to you from this? What necessity is there to judge me as impious and to trample on one who is suffering? You ought rather to pardon one who speaks under the pressure of pains. “Even if I had done such things as should not be done, was it right for you to reproach me in this way?” And, he says, “I who have long devoted myself to piety ought now to have confidence from my works. This I have not done, yet I am judged as one in error.” He adds this as well: Verses 6 and 7: “Know then that the Lord is the one who has troubled me, and he has raised his stronghold against me. Behold, I laugh at reproach; I will not speak. I will cry out, and there is no judgment anywhere.” Consider, he says: I am not afflicted without purpose, but I am surrounded by these terrors as if by a wall. I speak, he says, with truth, as my affairs really stand, and you do not accept my words. For “in reproach” means “the facts.” And “I will not speak” means: Because you contradict me, I seem to have said nothing. “And if I cry out to God, to bring my affairs into the open before all, I do not obtain my petition. No one hears, no one judges, I see no one, I have nowhere to go. Should these things not move pity?” “Therefore stop accusing me so rashly, lest God bring you into judgment, to exact from you the penalty for your unreasoning boldness.” For God, he says, does not leave such things unpunished. For he says it will happen, if he is moved against you, that your conceit about knowing the good and your security in what you possess will be shown to be useless. Aquila and Symmachus: “Why do you say that I suffer these things because I am in wickedness? You yourselves ought to fear the same things.” You would have been eager, he says, then, though the facts testify in words; so take your stand in words, as if not even by the truth would you vote me free from guilt. The Hebrew also has “a sin of the word.” Chapter 20, verse 10: “Let lesser men destroy his sons, and let his hands kindle pains.” And those who were previously inferior, he says, will prevail over the children of the lawless man. Verse 15: “Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited up; an angel will drag him out of his house.” The impious man does everything so as to take what belongs to others, and everything he does looks toward this goal. But when he thinks he has control of everything, then he will see himself transferred to others. Verse 18: “Like tough gristle, unchewed, not to be swallowed.” The words and doctrines of the impious man are twisted and bitter, for what is done against God has nothing sweet in it. Verse 22: “But when he thinks he is already filled, he will be afflicted, and every necessity will come upon him.” This is what he says: Because of this cause, what has been acquired is destroyed, and it is not passed on to descendants [Greek προγόνους, literally 'forebears']. Verse 23: “May he send upon him the fury of wrath, may he wash pains upon him.” This means: He will undergo terrors from God and from heaven. He said this because Job, having said that he was struck by God, also mentioned that he had been wronged by human beings. So he establishes that everything was brought upon him because of sins. Verse 25.
